title: Righteousness and Peace Have Kissed
superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.

verses.text: You showed favor to Your land, O LORD; You restored Jacob from captivity.
You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin. Selah
You withheld all Your fury; You turned from Your burning anger.
Restore us, O God of our salvation, and put away Your displeasure toward us.
Will You be angry with us forever? Will You draw out Your anger to all generations?
Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?
Show us Your loving devotion, O LORD, and grant us Your salvation.
I will listen to what God the LORD will say; for He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints; He will not let them return to folly.
Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him, that His glory may dwell in our land.
Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed.
Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven.
The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase.
Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps.

context.author: The title names the sons of Korah, a family of Levites descended from the Korah who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16). His sons did not die with him (Numbers 26:11), and their descendants became gatekeepers and singers at the Temple (1 Chronicles 9:19; 2 Chronicles 20:19).
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship, in times of national crisis
context.setting: The psalm remembers grace: “You showed favor to Your land, O LORD; You restored Jacob from captivity. You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin” (vv.1-2). Yet the people still live under God’s displeasure: “Restore us, O God of our salvation” (v.4). “Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?” (v.6). The psalmist waits: “I will listen to what God the LORD will say; for He will surely speak peace to His people” (v.8). Then comes a picture of salvation: “Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed. Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven” (vv.10-11). “The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase” (v.12).
context.custom: Many read the psalm after the return from Babylon, when the exiles were home but the land was poor and life was hard (Haggai 1:6-11; Nehemiah 9:36-37). The phrase “restored Jacob from captivity” can also mean a general turning of fortunes. A kiss was the greeting of family and friends and a sign of reconciliation (Genesis 33:4).
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 86, a prayer of David, asks God for an undivided heart.
context.timelineBible: At Jesus’ birth the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!” (Luke 2:14). Paul wrote, “since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1): righteousness and peace meet in Christ. The old wording of v.10, ‘mercy and truth are met together,’ made it a favorite Christmas text.

overview.summary: Remembering past forgiveness, the people ask God to revive them again, and wait to hear Him speak peace, until love and faithfulness meet and righteousness and peace kiss.

customs.t: A sign of welcome and reconciliation.
Good crops seen as God’s favor.

archaeology.t: Records Cyrus’ policy of returning deported peoples and their gods.
Seal impressions reading Yehud from the Persian province of Judah.

overview.discussion: “I will listen to what God the LORD will say” (v.8). How much of my prayer is speaking, and how much is listening?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-125 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: The sons of Korah
